query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an advanced free energy sampling framework—that combines high-fidelity first-principles calculations with kinetic Monte Carlo or molecular dynamics simulations—into the thermal processing design of as‐cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs will enable predictive control over phase evolution, resulting in a microstructure with a higher fraction of the targeted phase(s) and reduced formation of undesired phases.
generation.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA in the as‐cast or initially processed multiphase state with several constituent phases present.
generation.intervention: Implement a computationally driven thermal processing scheme based on an advanced free energy sampling framework to systematically map the free energy landscape as a function of processing parameters (e.g., annealing temperature, cooling rate, and pressure), and then use this information to tailor heat treatment protocols.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under controlled thermal treatment conditions; processing parameters (temperature, time, cooling rate, pressure) will be varied based on predictions from the free energy sampling framework.
generation.structural_mediator: Changes in the free energy landscape that modulate nucleation sites and phase boundary configurations, thereby directing the phase transformations.
generation.mechanism: By accurately mapping the free energy landscape, the framework predicts the thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic barriers associated with nucleation and growth of different phases. This allows targeted adjustment of processing conditions to favor the formation of desired phases while suppressing unwanted phase transformation pathways.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with traditional empirical thermal treatments, the framework-guided processing is expected to yield an alloy microstructure that is enriched in desired phases (e.g., a phase with optimized mechanical properties) and exhibits a lower overall fraction of unwanted secondary phases.
generation.baseline: Conventional thermal treatments where processing parameters are selected based on empirical methods without predictive free energy sampling.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable within the range of processing parameters and compositional variations typical for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs; its performance might be limited if diffusion kinetics or local compositional fluctuations introduce unforeseen complexities beyond the modeled free energy landscape.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the quantitative accuracy of predicting nucleation kinetics and phase fraction changes in the multicomponent free energy landscape, which requires further calibration against experimental data.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples. Process one set with conventional thermal treatments and another using processing conditions optimized by the advanced free energy sampling framework. Characterize the phases present in each sample using XRD, SEM, and TEM.
measurements: Phase fraction and distribution via X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Microstructural characterization using scanning/transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM)
Mechanical property evaluation (e.g., hardness, yield strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples processed using the free energy sampling-guided approach do not show a statistically significant improvement in the enrichment of the targeted phase(s) and reduction of undesired phases, as well as fail to exhibit enhanced mechanical properties compared to the conventionally processed samples, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

decision.trend: Early work on Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni-based HEAs, such as in PMC4999872, explored how non-equilibrium treatments (ion irradiation) affect phase stability and precipitation in multiphase alloys. This was followed by studies (PMC11087546) that leveraged advanced thermal treatments, including high-pressure and high-temperature processing, to deliberately modify microstructural phases and enhance mechanical performance. More recent work (PMC12806431) used controlled isothermal aging to trigger and tune phase transformations (e.g., tempering-like embrittlement and subsequent recovery), demonstrating that thermal processing conditions can systematically influence phase evolution. However, while these experimental approaches have demonstrated the sensitivity of phase evolution to processing parameters, they offer limited predictive control over the complex free energy landscape governing nucleation, growth, and phase stability in these alloys.
decision.unsolved: A key outstanding challenge is the precise, predictive control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs. Existing empirical thermal processing methods yield valuable insights but do not fully resolve how to tune processing conditions to consistently direct the phase transformations, due to the complex interplay of diffusion kinetics, nucleation barriers, and thermodynamic driving forces.
decision.lever: Implement an advanced free energy sampling framework that integrates high-fidelity first-principles calculations with kinetic Monte Carlo or molecular dynamics simulations. This approach would systematically map the free energy landscape as a function of key thermal processing parameters (e.g., annealing temperature, cooling rate, and pressure) to predict and optimize the nucleation and growth of desired phases.
decision.why: Building on the experimental observations that thermal treatments (from irradiation-induced changes to HPHT and aging regimes) significantly influence phase formation, this method offers a predictive tool to tailor processing conditions. It directly addresses the open question by enabling precise control over phase evolution, allowing designers to optimize the microstructure and properties of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
